title: Subjunctive or indicative?
why: This lesson answers the question every learner asks after meeting the subjunctive: when exactly do you need it? You learn to choose between indicative and subjunctive after opinions, feelings, doubt and possibility, and to avoid the classic traps espérer que, quand and après que.

{"lessons": ["

Opinions: the indicative by default

In the last lesson, the subjunctive came after wishes and necessity: il faut que, je veux que. Now the everyday question: after que, how do you know which mood to choose? Good news first. When you simply say what you think or believe, French uses the ordinary indicative, the forms you have known for months, present, past or future.

Opinion or certainty+ indicative
je pense que (I think that)Je pense qu'il a raison.
je crois que (I believe that)Je crois que Léa est malade.
il me semble que (it seems to me that)Il me semble que la boulangerie est fermée.
je suis sûr / sûre que (I'm sure that)Je suis sûre qu'elle viendra.
il est probable que (it's likely that)Il est probable qu'il pleuvra demain.

The switch: negation and inversion

As soon as the opinion becomes negative, or a question with inversion, the fact is no longer presented as true. It becomes uncertain, and French switches to the subjunctive. English changes nothing: \"I think he's right\", \"I don't think he's right\".

Je pense qu'il a raison. → Je ne pense pas qu'il ait raison.I think he's right. → I don't think he's right.
Je crois que c'est vrai. → Je ne crois pas que ce soit vrai.I believe it's true. → I don't believe it's true.
Penses-tu qu'elle puisse venir ?Do you think she can come?

In conversation, a question asked with simple intonation usually keeps the indicative: Tu penses qu'il va venir ? is perfectly natural. With inversion (Penses-tu que… ?, Croyez-vous que… ?) or with a negation, use the subjunctive.

", "

Feelings, doubt, possibility

The subjunctive is the mood of what you feel about a fact, of doubt, and of what is only possible. English uses an ordinary verb here (\"I'm glad you're here\"), so this is where English speakers slip. In French, the fact may be perfectly real: what counts is that the main verb expresses an emotion or a doubt.

TriggerExample
joy, sadnessje suis content / contente que, je suis triste queJe suis contente que tu sois là.
surprise, regretje suis surpris / surprise que, je regrette que, c'est dommage queC'est dommage que tu partes déjà.
fearj'ai peur queJ'ai peur qu'il fasse froid à Lille.
doubtje doute que, je ne suis pas sûr / sûre queJe doute qu'elle sache la réponse.
possibilityil est possible queIl est possible que nous soyons en retard.

Possible or probable?

The pair il est possible que / il est probable que shows the logic of the whole system. Something possible is uncertain: subjunctive. Something likely is almost a fact: indicative.

Il est possible qu'il pleuve. / Il est probable qu'il pleuvra.It might rain. / It will probably rain.

Careful with the false friend sans doute: it does not mean \"without a doubt\" but simply probably. Il viendra sans doute = he'll probably come. For real certainty, French says sans aucun doute.

After j'ai peur que, careful written French often adds a small ne that is not negative at all: J'ai peur qu'il ne pleuve means exactly the same as J'ai peur qu'il pleuve. Learn to recognize it; you don't need to use it.

", "

Three traps and one shortcut

Trap 1: espérer que + indicative

It looks like a wish, yet espérer que takes the indicative, very often the future. Its cousin souhaiter que takes the subjunctive. Learn the pair together.

espérer que + indicativesouhaiter que + subjunctive
J'espère que tu vas bien.Je souhaite que tu ailles mieux.
J'espère qu'il fera beau samedi.Je souhaite qu'il fasse beau samedi.

Trap 2: quand + future, never the subjunctive

Quand introduces a fact in time, not a doubt: Quand tu seras à Lyon, appelle-moi. English uses the present (\"when you are\"), French uses the future, and never the subjunctive.

Trap 3: après que + indicative

Avant que takes the subjunctive (the event has not happened yet), but in the norm après que takes the indicative (the event has happened): Après que les invités sont partis, on fait la vaisselle. You will often hear the subjunctive after après que; in an exercise, choose the indicative. Even simpler: après le départ des invités.

The shortcut: same subject → de + infinitive

As with vouloir, if both verbs have the same subject, drop que and use de + infinitive after feelings:

Je suis content de te voir. / Je suis content que tu sois là.I'm glad to see you. / I'm glad you're here.
J'ai peur de me tromper. / J'ai peur qu'il se trompe.I'm afraid of making a mistake. / I'm afraid he's making a mistake.

A quick test: is the main verb a simple opinion or a certainty, said positively? Indicative. Is it a negative opinion, an emotion, a doubt or a possibility? Subjunctive.
